slides.title: The method and why it is chosen
bullets: Haemoglobin concentration reflects the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood: a low value points to anaemia, a high one to polycythaemia.
The Tallqvist, Sahli and Lovibond methods are not sufficiently standardised and are therefore not recommended for clinical use.
The international committee for standardisation recommends the cyanmethaemoglobin method: all forms of haemoglobin except sulphaemoglobin are converted to haemoglobin cyanide.
After lysis of the red cells the colour of the solution is measured in a photometer; its intensity is directly proportional to the haemoglobin content.

slides.title: The method and why it is chosen
bullets: At least five minutes are needed for the reaction to go to completion.

slides.title: Reagent and equipment
bullets: A ready-made reagent kit (it contains potassium cyanide): light-sensitive, stored in a dark bottle; avoid direct sunlight.
Specimen: capillary blood or venous blood with K2-EDTA; capillary blood is measured promptly, venous blood within 6 hours of collection.
A calibrated blood pipette, a cuvette, a photometer/haemoglobinometer and a calibration table.
Each kit contains a standard (control) reagent; a central laboratory can also prepare and distribute it.

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 1. Switch the instrument on and check that it is set to the wavelength given in the reagent instructions (540–546 nm in the books).
2. Label the reagent tubes with the numbers from the patient’s requisition.
3. Fill the calibrated pipette with blood to the mark, check that there are no bubbles and that the blood is at the mark, and wipe the outside of the pipette.

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 4. Expel the blood into the reagent tube with a rubber bulb or an automatic pipette (never by mouth), rinse the pipette three times in the reagent; leave the tube undisturbed for at least five minutes.
5. Hold the clean cuvette without touching its sides with the fingers; zero the instrument on reagent without blood; rinse the cuvette with water.
6. Measure the control sample first, then the patient sample; rinse the cuvette with water before each measurement.

slides.title: Calculation of the result
bullets: Read the result from the calibration table using the instrument reading.
By factor: haemoglobin = absorbance of the sample × the factor printed on the reagent box (KF).
By standard blood: haemoglobin = (sample absorbance / standard absorbance) × haemoglobin concentration of the standard blood.
The linearity limit is given in the reagent instructions (50–240 g/L in the QVP book example); results above it call for a repeat measurement.
Units (g/L, g%) and reference intervals differ between the books, so the reagent instructions and the laboratory’s own ranges apply.

slides.title: Quality control
bullets: A standard (control) reagent is used every time a patient’s blood is tested; the result must match the known concentration of the control sample.
If enough reagent is available, testing two samples of the patient’s blood at once (or by two methods) is a good quality check.
If the results differ, the patient’s blood is tested again.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: The reagent is ready to use; usable until the stated date, kept at room temperature (10–30 °C).
Calibration: with standard blood (known haemoglobin) or by the K factor — the factor is given on the reagent box.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: Sample: capillary or venous blood with K2-EDTA; capillary blood is tested quickly, venous blood within 6 hours of collection.
The volumes are inconsistent in the source: sample 50.0 µL and reagent 1250 µL in the programme table, reagent 1.25 mL and blood 5 µL in the manual procedure — see the kit IFU.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: The values belong to the Hospitex Diagnostics kit and the Screen Master Plus photometer in the manual. The IFU of the kit you use and the analyser manual always take precedence — check the parameters against them.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: The reagent is poisonous (potassium cyanide): observe precautions when preparing, using and disposing of it.
Keep the reagent off skin and mucous membranes; for in vitro diagnostic use only.
Blood samples are potentially infectious: wear gloves and handle cuvettes and instruments with care.

slides.title: Why the Sahli method is not recommended
bullets: The Sahli (acid haematin), Tallqvist and Lovibond methods are not sufficiently standardised; the QVP book likewise does not recommend Sahli for clinical use today.
The Aripova book includes the Sahli method only because many laboratories cannot give it up for lack of funds; the first task of every laboratory is to replace it with the cyanmethaemoglobin method.
